summary_sentence: Every transformer variant tested outperforms both benchmarks. The release configuration, which combines temporal attention, cross-dyad attention and learned country embeddings, was selected because it achieved the lowest validation error; learned country identity improves forecasts in both validation and test, while the added value of cross-dyad attention, clear in validation, did not carry over to the more turbulent 2024–2026 test period.
path_sentence: Each of the three modelling changes contributed a similar amount (Figure 5, Table 3): stronger regularisation (+0.030), the residual formulation around the 52-week mean (+0.023) and the long-memory inputs (+0.023), with seed averaging adding +0.006. No single change was sufficient on its own; together they move the model from below the naive baseline to above gradient boosting. The regularisation gain reflects how quickly the original recipe overfitted: its best validation epoch was the eighth, with training loss far below validation loss.
ablation_paragraphs: The validation results are consistent with both expectations (Figure 6a). Removing cross-dyad attention raises validation error from 0.874 to 0.883, removing country embeddings raises it to 0.908, and removing both to 0.924, and the individual seeds follow the same ordering. On this evidence the protocol selected the full model as the release configuration.

The test period gives a more mixed picture (Figure 6b). Country embeddings help there as well: without them test R² falls from 0.639 to 0.631. Cross-dyad attention does not: the variant without it scores 0.646, slightly above the full model, with all three of its seeds above all three full-model seeds, and the purely row-by-row transformer (0.641) also edges ahead. These differences are small (under 0.01 R²) compared with the margin over the benchmarks, and every variant outperforms both the trailing mean and gradient boosting, so the value of the transformer approach as a whole holds in both periods. What the test period does not yet confirm is the specific added value of attending across the system.

Two explanations are plausible and not mutually exclusive. First, the test period was an unusually turbulent regime (the Gaza war, the Red Sea crisis and direct Israel–Iran exchanges), and system-level patterns learned from 2015–2022 may transfer less well than each relationship's own dynamics when the regional configuration itself shifts. Second, the long-memory inputs and residual formulation already give each dyad a strong summary of its own situation, leaving less for cross-dyad attention to add. We keep the full model as the release, since changing the architecture on the basis of test results would compromise the evaluation, and treat the transfer of system-level learning across regimes as a central question for the next version (Section 6).
conclusion: This section has demonstrated a new way of applying deep learning to forecasting international relations: each directed country pair becomes a token, a temporal transformer models each relationship's recent history, and a cross-dyad transformer forecasts the whole regional system jointly. Built on a single open data source and evaluated under a strict out-of-sample protocol, the prototype forecasts quarterly relations among 400 MENA dyads more accurately than naive forecasts and a strong gradient-boosting benchmark, runs live every two weeks, and supplies the likelihood component of the risk index developed elsewhere in this paper. The ablations sharpen the research agenda: learned country identity clearly helps, while the benefit of system-level attention, visible in validation, did not carry into the turbulent 2024–2026 test period. Text-based inputs from our own language models, more data through global scale-up, and attention structured around the network of active relationships are the natural next steps, and the framework built here is designed to test them.
